name: Question 4
problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}-4y=5{e}^{x}
$$

Consider the differential equation above, for which the corresponding complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-4x},$ where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants. Select the correct options below.$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{x}$ 
{{field-1}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{x}$ 
{{field-2}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The general solution of the differential equation is given by

$\,\,$
$y(x)=$ 
{{field-3}}
$+$
{{field-4}},

$\,$
where 
{{field-5}} are arbitrary constants.
worked_solution:
For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{c}(x)$ is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

- ${y}_{p}(x)$ is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

- For ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({e}^{x})^{′}={e}^{x}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =({e}^{x})^{′}={e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
({e}^{x})+3({e}^{x})-4({e}^{x})=5{e}^{x}.\,\,\times 
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{x}$ $\text{isn't}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

- For ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =(x{e}^{x})^{′}={e}^{x}+x{e}^{x}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =({e}^{x}+x{e}^{x})^{′}=2{e}^{x}+x{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
(2{e}^{x}+x{e}^{x})+3({e}^{x}+x{e}^{x})-4(x{e}^{x})=5{e}^{x}.\,\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{x}$ $\text{is}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-4x}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-4x}+x{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $A\text{ and }B$ are arbitrary constants.

EXPLANATION

For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x), where

  • yc(x) is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

  • yp(x) is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

  • For yp(x)=ex, we have y′(x)=(ex)′=ex,y″(x)=(ex)′=ex. Substituting this into the equation, we have (ex)+3(ex)−4(ex)=5ex.× So, yp(x)=ex isn't a particular solution of the differential equation.

  • For yp(x)=xex, we have y′(x)=(xex)′=ex+xex,y″(x)=(ex+xex)′=2ex+xex. Substituting this into the equation, we have (2ex+xex)+3(ex+xex)−4(xex)=5ex.✓ So, yp(x)=xex is a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is yc(x)=Aex+Be−4x. Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x)=Aex+Be−4x+xex where A and B are arbitrary constants.
